background.definition: Hidradenitis suppurativa (HS) is a recurrent disease affecting apocrine sweat gland-bearing skin. The disease course is characterized by occlusion of the apocrine gland duct followed by local inflammation and secondary infection. This process leads to the development of recurrent abscesses. Scarring and psychological effects can be significant. Systemic infection, skin cancer, and death have rarely been reported in association with HS.

list.listitem: Prevalence estimates vary from 0.53% to 4.1% of the general population.
Incidence appears to be increasing, as much as two-fold over the past 4 years. This may be due to changes in coding practices, improved recognition, and increased numbers of treatment procedures.
Pain, odor, poor body image, feeling of lack of control, and financial distress from work absence contribute to decreased quality of life.
Significant quality of life impairment occurs in multiple domains: self perception, daily living activities, mood, social functioning, and physical discomfort.
Psychosocial impact increases with more severe disease (Hurley stage II or III), earlier age of onset, and increasing pain severity.
Work absence is significantly higher in hidradenitis suppurativa patients.
Uncertain, but likely involves dysfunction of the follicular epithelium due to physical, genetic, and hormonal components.

Smoking is felt to be a strong triggering factor in patients genetically predisposed to develop HS. The prevalence of smoking in patients with HS is 88.9% in one study, with several other studies supporting an over 80% prevalence of smoking in patients with HS.

Previously thought to involve apocrine gland duct occlusion (with subsequent bacterial infection). However, most evidence supports initial follicular occlusion with secondary involvement of both apocrine and eccrine sweat glands as the central pathogenetic feature. Deficient follicular support structures may predispose to disease and provide direction for future research.
Local inflammation occurs, followed by secondary infection and abscess formation.
HS is associated with acanthosis nigricans, and authors have suggested an association with polycystic ovary syndrome.
Suspect HS in patients with tender nodular skin lesions in regions of skin folds especially with a history of recurrent symptoms, family history of HS, smoking, or female. C
Bacterial wound cultures may be useful for guiding antibiotic coverage in the acute setting. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Severe forms more common in males, affect face, chest, and back most commonly
Sexually transmitted, inguinal lymphadenopathy with headache fever migratory polymyalgias, and arthralgia
Inflammatory bowel disease associated with abscess formation
Recurrence of furuncles over weeks to months with lesions not focused to specific regions of the body
Cutaneous tuberculosis-firm, painless, SC nodules that gradually enlarge and suppurate
Subacute to chronic bacterial infection; contagious; formation of multiple abscesses most commonly cervicofacial, thoracic, and abdominal regions are affected

list.listitem: Early symptoms of HS include itching, burning, erythema, and discomfort.
The most common manifestation is tender nodular lesions in the axilla, perineum, perianal, buttocks, scrotum, or submammary regions. Multiple nodules are usually present.
Nodules may have malodorous drainage, which is usually polymicrobial when cultured.
Recurrent scarring disease with formation of fistulous tracts and incomplete healing increase the risk of bacterial contamination. Chronic draining sinus tracts from abscesses can form.
HS occurs most often in patients from puberty to 40 years of age.
Obtain history to include recurrent disease, family history, prior treatments, and psychological impact.
Physical examination should focus on the axillary, perineum, perianal, buttocks, scrotum, and submammary region.

British Association of Dermatologists guidelines (2018) recommend screening for depression, anxiety, and cardiovascular risk factors. If gastrointestinal symptoms are present evaluate for possible inflammatory bowel disease.
The diagnosis is made on clinical findings, but bacterial cultures may aid in selection of antibiotics.
Biopsy may be obtained to rule out other etiologies (eg, infected cystic acne), but is often not diagnostic.
Suspect HS in patients with tender nodular lesions in areas of skin folds especially if recurrent. Increased likelihood when patient is a smoker, female, or has a family history of HS.
In early stages of the disease, purulent material is often sterile. As the disease progresses, various pathogens may be found. Consider culturing if sinus tract formation or scarring have occurred.
Empiric therapy includes topical clindamycin.
General measures should include smoking cessation and weight reduction for patients with obesity. C
Topical clindamycin improves healing rates and reduces recurrences. B
For mild to moderate HS, prospective cohort studies and guidelines support using oral tetracyclines as first-line, and clindamycin + rifampin as second-line treatment.B
For moderate to severe HS, adalimumab is the first-line biologic treatment, while infliximab is recommended for second-line therapy.B
Use of a multidisciplinary approach including primary care physician, skin specialist, and psychologist is recommended. C

Guidelines from the British Association of Dermatologists (2018) recommend initially prescribing a tetracycline for 12 weeks. For patients unresponsive to tetracyclines, consider the combination of oral clindamycin 300 mg twice daily and rifampicin 300 mg twice daily for 10–12 weeks.

The BAD guidelines also recommend considering acitretin 0 3–0 5 mg kg 1 day 1 in males and nonfertile females or dapsone in patients who are unresponsive to antibiotic therapies. They recommend adalimumab 40 mg weekly for patients in whom these conventional therapies are unsuccessful. If adalimumab is not successful, they recommend infliximab 5 mg/kg every 8 weeks.
Few studies of medical treatment for HS exist and most involve small populations. Topical clindamycin has been shown to have an effect in a double-blind placebo-controlled study.

Prospective cohort studies and guidelines support using oral tetracyclines as first-line, and oral clindamycin + rifampin as second-line treatment. The largest study is a 12-week European prospective cohort trial (N = 283) evaluating oral tetracyclines (i.e., tetracycline, N = 42, doxycycline, N = 121, and minocycline, N = 17) versus oral clindamycin + rifampin (N = 103). It found similar efficacy between tetracyclines and clindamycin + rifampin, regardless of disease severity.

Multiple small studies have investigated other medical treatments with favorable results, including finasteride, isotretinoin, and infliximab. A case series of 8 patients treated with infliximab suggested significant improvement in dermatology life quality index (DLQI) scores at 12 months of therapy. All of these studies recommended further evaluation with RCTs to further assess effectiveness of therapy. A systematic review of systemic therapies found limited evidence overall, but concluded that infliximab and adalimumab were the most effective agents. However, the author had financial ties to the two companies that manufacture those two drugs, and the systematic review did not follow the usual protocol for such studies.

A systematic review concluded that clindamycin and rifampin (combined), monthly Nd:YAG laser treatments, surgical excision and primary closure with a gentamicin sulfate-collagen sponge, and infliximab were likely to be effective.
Practice guidelines can improve the appropriateness of antibiotic selection, without adversely affecting clinical outcomes.
See also chapter on "Carbuncle, furuncle and other skin abscess."

A randomized trial treated 154 moderate to severe HS patients with adalimumab 40 mg/week or alternate weeks or placebo. At week 16, 3.9% placebo, 9.6% alternate week therapy and 17.6% weekly adalimumab patients achieved primary outcome response of HS-PGA score of clear, minimal or mild disease with at least 2-grade improvement from baseline. Significantly greater improvement in patient-reported outcomes and pain were seen in the weekly dosing group compared to placebo.Two larger randomized trials with a total of 633 patients similarly found benefit from adalimumab. A Cochrane review similarly showed quality-of-life improvements with adalimumab and infliximab.

A study randomized 103 patients with moderate to severe HS who were about to undergo wide excisional surgery to adalimumab or placebo during the perioperative period (24 weeks total). The intervention group had a significantly higher likelihood of treatment response (48% vs 34%, NNT = 7).

A double-blind placebo trial of 20 patients with anakinra, IL 1 inhibitor, in a 12-week treatment and 12-week follow-up phase, decreased disease activity scores at the end of treatment in 20% of placebo compared with 67% with anakinra (p = 0.04), with clinical response of 30% and 78% in both groups (p = 0.04). No serious side effects were reported.

An RCT in 20 patients with moderate HS compared 30 mg twice daily apremilast and placebo at 16 weeks. 53% showed a clinical response (p = 0.055) and the apremilast group showed a significantly lower abscess and nodule count (0 = 0.011). There was no significant difference in quality of life DLQI scores. Most frequent side effects were headache and GI symptoms.

Few studies of surgical treatment for HS exist and most involve small case series. Surgical options included simple incision and drainage of abscesses, deroofing using punch technique, electrosurgical and cryosurgical procedures, and wide excision of full-thickness skin with musculocutaneous skin flap placement.
Wide excision is recommended by British Academy of Dermatolists guidelines (2018) when conventional systemic treatments fail to reduce the recurrence rate.
Ultrasound-guided needle aspiration is inferior to traditional incision and drainage, based on a small RCT with 101 patients.
Weak evidence suggests less recurrence of HS with more aggressive surgical options, but with an increased risk of surgical complications.

Intense pulsed light therapy was evaluated in a trial of 18 patients utilizing contralateral involved body sites as controls evaluated by a non-treating physician with a clinical scoring system and patient satisfaction rated on a Likert scale. Significant reduction in clinical severity scores as well as increased patient satisfaction were noted. Limitations included small number of patients, absence of a more robust quality-of-life measurement, and absence of intention to treat (one patient dropped out after one treatment and was not included in analyses).

A case series of 12 patients with specific IgG reaction to brewer's yeast treated with surgical resection of axillary and perineal fistulas and a brewer's yeast exclusion diet demonstrated improved quality of life as well as recurrence of disease after accidental or voluntary consumption of brewer's yeast or wheat-containing foods during a 12-month follow-up period.
Smoking cessation may be effective in reducing disease activity and should be encouraged as a general health measure in any case.
Warm compresses or hydrotherapy are usually recommended, but studies of effectiveness are lacking.

British Academy of Dermatolists guidelines (2018) recommend that intralesional corticosteroid injections be considered for selected patients during the acute phase. The guidelines recommend against cryotherapy or microwave ablation.
Consider a multidisciplinary approach including the primary care physician, with possibly dermatology, plastic surgery, and psychology if appropriate for the individual patient.
Reports of local/regional recurrence rates up to 100% for surgical drainage alone and up to 25% for radical excision are found in the surgical literature. C
Physical scarring, including emotional and social stress, is often debilitating. C
One small cohort study of 73 patients with HS reported an increased incidence of nonmelanoma skin cancer (RR = 1.5–10.7). C
